rows: A scorpion's eyes can apparently take in the whole way around its body. The two middle eyes together cover a full circle, with about forty degrees of overlap above the animal.

The pair of eyes in the middle of the head are the main eyes. They give a fairly sharp picture and tell shapes apart. The side eyes, three to five pairs, seem to notice mostly changes in how bright the light is.
Buthid scorpions have five pairs of small side eyes. The first three are about 0.3 mm across and the last two are about 0.12 mm across in one species.

Electrical recordings from the eyes of two scorpion genera peak in blue light at 470 nanometres and in green light at 525. The recordings do not say how many kinds of receptor lie behind the two peaks. The side eyes also respond in the ultraviolet.
Scorpions are active at night and their eyes can sense starlight. In one species the middle eyes are about a thousand times more sensitive at night than by day.

No record gives how much detail a scorpion sees, so this view shows a coarse picture. The extra brightness, the recolouring from two colour peaks, and the way the all-round view is pressed into the phone are the app's own.

A scorpion feels the ground through its legs and can locate prey up to about 50 cm away by the waves it makes in sand. It tastes the air and ground with its comb-like pectines and feels wind with fine hairs. The camera records none of this.
Some settings in this view are the app's own choices, because no measurement gives them. They are set to give a fair picture of the animal and can be tuned by hand.

rows.title: All around
rows.text: A review states that, based on physiological evidence, scorpions can apparently see 360 degrees around their bodies, a full circle. Nobody has measured how far around you your own eyes see.
rows.note: R1 is a review's statement about scorpions as a group, so I kept it as a statement from a review and said it is unmeasured in your species.

rows.title: Two kinds of eyes
rows.text: You have two kinds of eyes, median and lateral. A review of scorpion eyes says the median eyes may form low-resolution images, while the lateral eyes are highly sensitive to light but have no lens that focuses an image. Nobody has measured what either kind does in your species.
rows.note: Left out R1 (a whipscorpion, a different order) and the numbers in R2 and R3, since they belong to single species. Replaced "reports" with "says".

rows.title: Many small eyes
rows.text: Along each side of the front of your body sit several small eyes. A survey of 20 species in the family Buthidae, which includes the bark scorpions, found 5 pairs of these side eyes, where earlier works had counted only 3 pairs. Nobody has measured how many side eyes you have in your own species, so that count is still unknown.
rows.note: R1 is a family-level survey that does not name the species counted, so the count stays open for each listed species. I left out the specimen total and any claim about the median eyes, which no record covers.

rows.title: Blue and green
rows.text: Your eyes may sense blue and green light best of all. In Edward's bark scorpion, electrical recordings from the median and side eyes peak at blue (470 nanometers) and green (525 nanometers) and drop much lower for yellow and ultraviolet, and you very likely match it if you are another bark scorpion of the genus Centruroides. Nobody has measured which colors the eyes of other scorpions sense best.
rows.note: Only one species (Edward's bark scorpion) is measured; the record gives peak wavelengths but no count of color-sensing cell types, so I made no claim about color vision.

rows.title: Eyes for the night
rows.text: If you are an Androctonus australis, your two median eyes are about 1,000 times more sensitive to light at night than by day, and this daily rhythm keeps going even in constant darkness. A review of scorpion eyes says the median eyes of some desert scorpions may see well enough to use the horizon for orientation, even on moonless nights. For every other scorpion, nobody has measured how little light your eyes need.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "says". Left out the review's pigment-migration claim because its quote does not state it. Only Androctonus australis is measured.

rows.title: The ground and the air
rows.text: If you are a sand-dwelling scorpion, Paruroctonus mesaensis, slit-shaped sense organs on your legs respond to ripples in the sand made by insects up to 50 centimeters away, according to a paper's abstract. A review says the sensory hairs and trichobothria of scorpions react to air streams and are sensitive to the direction the air comes from. Nobody has measured either sense in most scorpions, so how far your own legs and hairs reach is unknown.
rows.note: Left out R1, R2 and R5 (R1 and R2 are single-species behavior tests; R5 repeats R3). R3 is from an abstract and R4 from a review, so the row says so.
